lesson.title: Moving Bytes: How Send and Receive Actually Work
lesson.summary: The send and receive operations are the fundamental calls that move data across a socket, and understanding their quirks, like partial transfers, is essential before building anything on top of them.
lesson.body:
Once a TCP socket is connected, or a UDP socket has somewhere to send to, everything a program does boils down to two operations: send data out, and receive data in. On most systems these are exposed as send() and recv() (many platforms also let the plain write() and read() calls work on socket file descriptors, since the operating system treats them the same as other file descriptors). It is tempting to think of send() as handing the network an exact buffer that arrives as one unit, but that is not how the underlying model works, especially for TCP.

For a TCP socket, the connection provides an ordered, reliable stream of bytes, not a sequence of discrete messages. When a program calls send() with 5000 bytes, the operating system is not obligated to transmit all 5000 bytes as a single unit, nor is it obligated to even accept all 5000 bytes into its send buffer in one call. send() can return having only queued part of the data, a short write, and the caller is responsible for checking the return value and calling send() again with whatever bytes are left. Symmetrically, recv() on the receiving end might return 3000 bytes on one call and the remaining 2000 on a second call, or it might combine data from two separate send() calls into a single recv() call. TCP does not preserve message boundaries. The stream only guarantees that bytes arrive in order and without gaps, not that the chunks a program wrote line up with the chunks it later reads.

UDP sockets behave differently. Each send() call produces exactly one datagram, and each recv() call returns exactly one datagram, or none if none has arrived, and the boundary of that datagram is preserved from sender to receiver. There is no partial delivery to manage the way TCP requires, though a UDP datagram can still be dropped entirely, arrive out of order, or arrive duplicated, since UDP does not provide the ordering and reliability guarantees that TCP does.

This distinction is why real networking code almost always wraps the raw send and receive calls in a loop. For TCP, a helper function typically keeps calling send() until every byte has actually been queued, and keeps calling recv() until either enough bytes have arrived or the connection has closed. Skipping this step, and assuming a single call moves one complete message, is one of the most common bugs in early networked code. It usually appears to work fine with small test messages and only breaks once messages grow larger than a single TCP segment, or once the network is under real load.
